chapter: 第4章 讲座或讲话
title: Test 1 · 讲座或讲话
en:
Lecture One (Questions 16–18)

America continues to lead the world as a destination for international students. Last year, about 900,000 foreign students were studying in the United States, about half of them from Asia. But a growing number of Asian students are looking to an English-speaking country much closer to home: the Philippines. The island nation of 100 million is quickly becoming the education center of Asia. The country's low prices, open culture and quality schools are attracting record numbers of foreign students.

Koreans are leading the way, according to Jose El Quesia, the Philippines ambassador to the United States. The Philippines is in a unique position to benefit from the global demand for English education. American colonialism brought the English language here in the early 20th century. Although it is not the native language of most Filipinos, English is an official language here. More than 60 years after independence, Filipinos still speak English with a strong American accent. Today, the Philippines markets itself as the world's third-largest English-speaking country. The truth is, there are actually more people who speak English in the Philippines than the national language. English is learned even outside of school, because a lot of the communications are done in English — public signs are in English, television and internet are all in English.

Low prices and its location in Asia helped to produce the education explosion in the Philippines. The capital, Manila, has cheap nonstop flights to Tokyo, Seoul and other Asian capitals. The rising US dollar has made American education more expensive than ever before.

There are hundreds of private and public schools in the Philippines that teach English or teach in English. More advanced students can take regular university academic courses in English. Others study at beachside resorts, where they mix language study with vacation. Some Korean families even moved to the Philippines so that children can learn English in public schools.

As in the US, schools in the Philippines range from world class to low-quality diploma mills. In most Asian countries, students learn English through grammar and translation from the mother language. In the Philippines, students are encouraged to practice speaking English in real-life situations. In general, there is less emphasis on grammar and error correction. In the Philippines, you can see English everywhere — on the signs, in businesses and offices, and in schools.

Lecture Two (Questions 19–22)

Bitcoin is a digital currency used by terrorists and drug dealers as well as major companies like Microsoft and Overstock.com. In other words, everyone from private individuals who order pizza to terrorists who order weapons. Bitcoin was a currency created in 2009 by a mysterious software developer who calls himself Satoshi Nakamoto. No one has ever met him, and it is not clear if he is one person or several people.

Bitcoin does not use printed money. It is digital only. The currency is created on computers by a community of people across the globe. Anyone can join that network or group, according to CoinDesk.com. This network processes transactions made with the digital currency. Bitcoins are stored in a digital wallet, over the internet or on the user's computer.

There is not an unlimited amount of bitcoins. Nakamoto set up rules to limit the currency to 21 million bitcoins. With bitcoins, there are no banks or fees. Users do not register with their real names. Merchandise can be bought without the user showing her or his identity. Bitcoins are not taxed or regulated anywhere in the world.

Bitcoins have become the currency of choice for people online buying drugs or other illegal activities. For example, bitcoins are being used by ISIS terrorists to fund operations, according to Ghost Security Group, a counterterrorism network that focuses on the internet and social media. Morgan Wright is a cybersecurity expert and senior fellow at the Center for Digital Government, a national research and advisory institute on information technology policies. "Terrorists need anonymity," Wright told Fox News. "Countries have gotten very good at tracking terror financing in the years since 9/11. Networks have looked for new ways to do it, and it appears they've found it in Bitcoin."

Despite this dark side of the new currency, bitcoins have their supporters. More and more merchants are beginning to accept bitcoins. Some people buy bitcoins as an investment, hoping they'll increase in value. There are many online marketplaces that allow people to buy and sell bitcoins using different currencies. Coinbase in San Francisco runs the world's largest Bitcoin exchange and operates 2.8 million Bitcoin wallets globally. According to Wired, you can also buy and sell bitcoins on BitQuick, Zapoo and CoinCorner, among other exchanges. It is possible to do complex financial trades with bitcoins, such as futures, options and swaps.

The price of bitcoins on online exchanges has fluctuated widely, which has led to speculation in the digital currency. In 2009 and early 2010, bitcoins had no value at all, said Wired. Then in late 2013 it reached a high of 1,216 dollars. As of now, the price of one Bitcoin is about 434 dollars.

Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

Good morning. I'm Mario Ritter. Today I am going to talk about how to make an effective complaint.

When a consumer finds that an item she or he bought is faulty or in some other way does not live up to the manufacturer's claims, the first step is to present the warranty or any other records which might help at the store of purchase. In most cases, this action will produce results. However, if it does not, there are various means the consumer may use to gain satisfaction.

A simple and common method used by many consumers is to complain directly to the store manager. In general, the higher up his or her complaint, the faster he or she can expect it to be settled. In such a case, it is usually settled in the consumer's favor, assuming he or she has a just claim.

Consumers should complain in person whenever possible, but if they cannot get to the place of purchase, it is acceptable to phone or write the complaint in a letter.

Complaining is usually most effective when it is done politely but firmly, and especially when the consumer can demonstrate what is wrong with the item in question. If this cannot be done, the consumer will succeed best by presenting specific information as to what is wrong rather than by making general statements. For example, "the left speaker does not work at all and the sound coming out of the right one is unclear" is better than "this stereo does not work."

The store manager may advise the consumer to write to the manufacturer. If so, the consumer should do this, stating the complaint as politely and firmly as possible. If a polite complaint does not achieve the desired result, the consumer can go a step further. She or he can threaten to take the seller to court or report the seller to a private or public organization responsible for protecting consumers' rights.

Questions

16. What do we learn about the Philippines?
17. What do we learn about the English language in the Philippines?
18. How do students learn English in the Philippines?
19. What do we learn about Bitcoin?
20. Why are bitcoins favored by terrorists, according to Morgan Wright?
21. Who runs the largest Bitcoin exchange in the world?
22. What was the price of one Bitcoin in late 2013?
23. What should a consumer first do when he finds the item he bought is faulty?
24. How can a consumer make his complaint more effective?
25. What may the manager advise the consumer to do?
zh:
讲座一（第 16—18 题）

美国仍然是全球国际学生的首选目的地。去年约有 90 万外国学生在美国学习，其中约一半来自亚洲。但越来越多的亚洲学生把目光投向离家乡近得多的英语国家：菲律宾。这个拥有一亿人口的岛国正迅速成为亚洲的教育中心。低廉的价格、开放的文化和高质量的学校，正吸引创纪录数量的外国学生。

菲律宾驻美大使何塞·埃尔·克西亚说，韩国人走在了前头。菲律宾处于独特位置，可以从全球英语教育需求中受益。20 世纪初，美国的殖民统治把英语带到了这里。虽然英语不是大多数菲律宾人的母语，却是这里的官方语言之一。独立 60 多年后，菲律宾人讲英语仍带着浓重的美国口音。今天，菲律宾把自己宣传为世界第三大英语国家。事实是，菲律宾讲英语的人实际上比讲国语的人还多。英语甚至在校外也能学到，因为很多交流都用英语——公共标牌是英语，电视和互联网也全是英语。

低廉的价格和地处亚洲的位置，促成了菲律宾的教育热潮。首都马尼拉有直飞东京、首尔等亚洲首都的廉价航班。而美元升值使美国教育比以往任何时候都更贵。

菲律宾有数百所公立和私立学校用英语教学或以英语授课。水平较高的学生可以修读正规大学的英语学术课程。另一些人则在海滨度假村学习，把语言学习和度假结合起来。有些韩国家庭甚至搬到菲律宾，好让孩子在公立学校学英语。

和美国一样，菲律宾的学校从世界一流到低劣的「文凭工厂」都有。在大多数亚洲国家，学生通过语法讲解和从母语翻译来学英语；而在菲律宾，学生被鼓励在真实情境中练习说英语，总体上对语法和纠错的强调较少。在菲律宾，你到处都能看到英语——在标牌上、在企业和办公室里、在学校里。

讲座二（第 19—22 题）

比特币是一种数字货币，使用者既有恐怖分子和毒贩，也有微软、Overstock.com 这样的大公司。换句话说，从点披萨的普通人到订购武器的恐怖分子，都在用。比特币是 2009 年由一位自称中本聪的神秘软件开发者创造的货币。没有人见过他，也不清楚他是一个人还是几个人。

比特币不使用印制的钞票，只存在于数字世界。这种货币由全球各地的一群人用计算机「挖」出来。据 CoinDesk.com 介绍，任何人都可以加入这个网络或群体。这个网络处理用这种数字货币进行的交易。比特币存放在数字钱包里——在互联网上或在用户自己的电脑上。

比特币的数量不是无限的。中本聪设定了规则，把总量限制在 2100 万个。使用比特币没有银行、没有手续费。用户不用真名注册。购买商品时无需出示身份。比特币在世界上任何地方都不被征税，也不受监管。

比特币已成为网上购买毒品或其他非法活动的人的首选货币。例如，据「幽灵安全小组」称，ISIS 恐怖分子正用比特币为行动筹资——该小组是一个专注于互联网和社交媒体的反恐网络。摩根·赖特是一位网络安全专家，也是数字政府中心的高级研究员，该中心是一家研究信息技术政策的全国性研究与咨询机构。「恐怖分子需要匿名，」赖特对福克斯新闻说，「9·11 之后的这些年里，各国在追踪恐怖融资方面已经非常擅长。网络组织一直在寻找新的办法，看来他们在比特币里找到了。」

尽管这种新货币有黑暗的一面，比特币仍有支持者。越来越多的商家开始接受比特币。有些人把比特币当作投资买进，希望它升值。有很多在线市场可以让人们用不同货币买卖比特币。旧金山的 Coinbase 运营着全球最大的比特币交易所，在全世界运营着 280 万个比特币钱包。据《连线》杂志报道，你还可以在 BitQuick、Zapoo 和 CoinCorner 等交易所买卖比特币。用比特币还可以做复杂的金融交易，比如期货、期权和互换。

在线交易所上比特币的价格波动很大，这引发了这种数字货币的投机。《连线》称，2009 年和 2010 年初，比特币一文不值；到 2013 年末，它涨到 1216 美元的高点。目前，一枚比特币的价格约为 434 美元。

讲座三（第 23—25 题）

早上好，我是马里奥·里特。今天我要讲的是如何有效地投诉。

当消费者发现自己购买的商品有缺陷，或以其他方式不符合厂商的宣称时，第一步是在购买该商品的商店出示保修单或任何可能有帮助的记录。大多数情况下，这一做法就会奏效。但如果无效，消费者还可以用各种方式争取满意的结果。

许多消费者采用的一种简单而常见的办法，是直接向店长投诉。一般说来，投诉的层级越高，问题解决得越快。在这种情况下，只要消费者的要求正当，通常会以有利于消费者的方式解决。

消费者应尽可能当面投诉；如果去不了购买地点，打电话或写信投诉也可以。

投诉时礼貌而坚定通常最有效，尤其是当消费者能说明商品到底哪里有问题时。如果做不到这一点，消费者最好陈述具体的问题信息，而不是做笼统的表述。例如，「左边的音箱完全不响，右边音箱出来的声音不清楚」，就比「这台音响坏了」要好。

店长可能会建议消费者写信给厂家。如果是这样，消费者就应该照做，并尽可能礼貌而坚定地说明投诉内容。如果礼貌的投诉没有达到预期效果，消费者可以再进一步：威胁把卖方告上法庭，或向负责保护消费者权益的私立或公立机构举报卖方。

题目

16. 关于菲律宾我们了解到什么？
17. 关于菲律宾的英语我们了解到什么？
18. 菲律宾的学生怎样学英语？
19. 关于比特币我们了解到什么？
20. 按摩根·赖特的说法，比特币为什么受恐怖分子青睐？
21. 谁在运营世界上最大的比特币交易所？
22. 2013 年末一枚比特币的价格是多少？
23. 消费者发现购买的商品有缺陷时，首先应该做什么？
24. 消费者怎样才能让投诉更有效？
25. 店长可能会建议消费者做什么？

chapter: 第4章 讲座或讲话
title: Test 2 · 讲座或讲话
en:
Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

Today we have good news for all our coffee drinkers around the world. A new study finds that drinking coffee can help you live longer. Researchers at the Harvard School of Public Health recently discovered that drinking between three and five cups of coffee a day may prevent certain illnesses. They found that coffee can protect against heart disease, brain diseases and suicide.

Walter Willett is a nutrition researcher at Harvard and co-author of the study.
— Professor Willett, thank you for joining us.
— Good morning.
— The findings of our study extend to both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee — or "decaf," as Americans often call it. The health benefits come not just from the caffeine in coffee, but from the compounds in the beans. Our study was large — about 200,000 subjects — and included data from three ongoing studies. Subjects in the study had to answer questions about their coffee drinking habits every four years over a 30-year period. We found that moderate coffee drinking was linked with a reduced risk of death from many diseases. However, we found no link between coffee drinking and cancer. We also considered other habits such as smoking, obesity and how active the subjects were. We also looked at what kinds of food the subjects ate, as well as how much alcohol and what type of alcohol they drank.

"Our research adds to a growing body of evidence." This body of evidence finds drinking a moderate amount of coffee may have many health benefits, including a longer life. This is according to one of the researchers involved in the study, Frank Hu, who is the senior author of the study. He is also a professor of nutrition and epidemiology. He studied how food affects illness. Hu adds the data from the study support that drinking a moderate amount of coffee can be part of a healthy diet, but how much and when you drink coffee is important.

Nevertheless, our study also received doubts and criticism. Andrew Maynard of Arizona State University claims that the health benefits documented in this new study are small. Maynard says the study does not prove cause and effect between drinking coffee and living longer; he says the study does point to an association or link between drinking coffee and living longer.

"Honestly speaking, I am personally not sure how coffee is linked to certain health benefits. So what I can give you as the take-home message — in other words, the important thing to learn — is that if you like coffee, do not feel guilty about drinking it in moderation. If you don't like coffee, don't feel you have to start drinking it to be healthy." Thank you very much.

Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

Many people who drink alcohol also like to smoke cigarettes. Drinking and smoking seem to be closely linked. Some people might even say they go together hand in hand. But this may be more than just a mixing of two fairly common activities.

New research has looked more closely at the relationship between cigarettes and alcohol. And the relationship is one of equal dependence. Smoking and drinking seem to feed on each other. These are the exact words of Mahesh Thakar. He is head of research in the Department of Neurology at the University of Missouri's School of Medicine.

Thakar explains that when a person drinks alcohol, they get sleepy. He says a drug in cigarettes fights that sleepy feeling. That drug, nicotine, can be addictive. Smokers need more cigarettes because of their body's growing dependence on the drug. So if a person smokes, then he or she is much more likely to drink alcohol, and vice versa. Thakar says they feed off one another.

Researchers already knew that people who use alcohol often smoke. In fact, earlier research shows that more than 85% of alcohol-dependent American adults also depend on nicotine. Thakar's earlier research showed that nicotine combined with alcohol stimulates what he calls the reward center of the brain. However, the new study shows a dependent relationship between the substances.

Thakar says his team found that nicotine weakens the sleep-causing effects of alcohol. It does this by activating an area of the brain called the basal forebrain. According to the Psychology Definition website, that area is responsible for memory, learning and attention.

For this new experiment, Thakar and his team used equipment that measures brain activity in rats. They injected the rats with both nicotine and alcohol and then studied brain activity in the animals as they slept. The researchers found that nicotine goes through the basal forebrain and cancels out the sleep-causing effects of alcohol.

So why is this new research important? The World Health Organization says 7 million people die every year from alcohol and nicotine use. Mahesh Thakar and his team identified why alcohol use and smoking are often linked. He says this knowledge may help people break their addictions to alcohol and nicotine. The researchers published their findings in the Journal of Neurochemistry.

Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

Until recently, blind and visually impaired students in Kenya were still using Braille books for their studies. But Kenyan schools for the blind are now beginning to adopt technology that provides material in an audible form — and in the process expands their opportunities.

Lucas Munzia intently searches the internet for information. Today's class is on biology. Munzia is visually impaired and for the last two years has been attending computer classes at the Thika School for the Blind. Munzia is in eighth grade, having started school at a later age because of his vision. He says the technology has opened up new frontiers that were once inaccessible.

"Braille books are quite expensive and you have to use quite a sum to purchase one," Munzia explained. "But now, since we have computers, we get the books at virtually no cost. So we download the various books to read and, when we are done, we just close the program."

The school embraced assistive technology six years ago, enabling blind and visually impaired students to access information from computers and iPads. Zachary Muiza, one of the school's teachers, was born blind. He has been teaching the students how to use the technology for about two years now. He says the technology presents opportunities that can level the playing field for his students.

"Assistive technology equips the learners with very many skills that really make them independent in life," he said. "They can read materials like books, magazines, newspapers by themselves. And apart from that, assistive technology equips them with employable skills."

The assistive technology costs 1,000 dollars for a school to install, but an NGO called Enable has provided it to the schools at no cost. Peter Oao, the program manager at Enable, says blind students using the technology may still face challenges when they move to higher education.

"When learners move from primary to high school and then to universities, they go to university and then they realize there is not that technology. So the fact is that they learned that technology in primary and high school. When they move to university, they go back to Braille, which is another challenge to them."

So far, four out of Kenya's 11 schools for the blind have adopted the technology. Enable says it will provide the funding for the remaining schools to come on board.

Questions

21. What do we know about nicotine?

zh:
讲座一（第 16—19 题）

今天，我们要给全世界喝咖啡的人带来一个好消息。一项新研究发现，喝咖啡有助于长寿。哈佛大学公共卫生学院的研究人员最近发现，每天喝三到五杯咖啡可能预防某些疾病。他们发现，咖啡能预防心脏病、脑部疾病和自杀。

沃尔特·威利特是哈佛的营养学研究者，也是这项研究的合著者。
—— 威利特教授，感谢您接受采访。
—— 早上好。
—— 我们的研究结论同时适用于含咖啡因和不含咖啡因的咖啡（美国人常说的「decaf」）。健康益处不仅来自咖啡中的咖啡因，也来自咖啡豆里的化合物。我们的研究规模很大，约 20 万名受试者，纳入了三项正在进行的研究的数据。受试者要在 30 年间每四年回答一次关于自己喝咖啡习惯的问题。我们发现，适度喝咖啡与死于多种疾病的风险降低有关。不过，我们没有发现喝咖啡与癌症之间有关联。我们还考虑了吸烟、肥胖、受试者的活动量等其他习惯，也考察了受试者吃什么食物、喝多少酒以及喝什么酒。

「我们的研究为一组不断积累的证据增添了新内容。」这些证据表明，适量喝咖啡可能有许多健康益处，包括更长的寿命。这番话出自参与该研究的研究者之一、该研究的资深作者弗兰克·胡。他也是营养学与流行病学教授，研究食物如何影响疾病。胡补充说，研究数据支持「适量喝咖啡可以成为健康饮食的一部分」，但喝多少、什么时候喝很重要。

不过，我们的研究也受到质疑和批评。亚利桑那州立大学的安德鲁·梅纳德声称，这项新研究记录的健康益处很微小。梅纳德说，该研究并未证明喝咖啡与更长寿之间的因果关系；他说，研究确实表明喝咖啡与更长寿之间存在相关性或关联。

「说实话，我个人并不确定咖啡是如何与某些健康益处联系起来的。所以我能给你的『要点』——也就是最该记住的东西——是：如果你喜欢咖啡，不必因为适度饮用而感到内疚；如果你不喜欢咖啡，也不必觉得为了健康非得开始喝。」非常感谢。

讲座二（第 20—22 题）

许多喝酒的人也喜欢抽烟。喝酒和吸烟似乎关系密切，有些人甚至会说它们形影不离。但这可能不只是两种相当常见行为的叠加。

新研究更仔细地考察了香烟与酒精之间的关系。这是一种相互依赖的关系：吸烟与饮酒似乎在相互「喂养」。这是马赫什·塔卡尔的原话。他是密苏里大学医学院神经学系研究主管。

塔卡尔解释说，人喝酒后会犯困；香烟中的一种物质会对抗这种困意。这种物质就是尼古丁，而尼古丁会成瘾。由于身体对这种物质日益依赖，吸烟者需要抽更多的烟。所以，如果一个人吸烟，他（她）喝酒的可能性就大得多，反之亦然。塔卡尔说，它们相互喂养。

研究人员早已知道，喝酒的人常常吸烟。事实上，早期研究显示，85% 以上酒精依赖的美国成年人同时也依赖尼古丁。塔卡尔早期的研究显示，尼古丁与酒精结合会刺激他所说的「大脑奖赏中枢」。而这项新研究显示，这两种物质之间存在依赖关系。

塔卡尔说，他的团队发现尼古丁会削弱酒精的催眠作用。它是通过激活大脑中一个叫「基底前脑」的区域来实现的。据「心理学定义」网站介绍，该区域负责记忆、学习和注意力。

在这项新实验中，塔卡尔和团队使用了测量大鼠大脑活动的设备。他们给大鼠同时注射尼古丁和酒精，然后研究动物睡眠时的大脑活动。研究者发现，尼古丁会经过基底前脑，抵消酒精的催眠作用。

那么这项新研究为什么重要？世界卫生组织称，每年有 700 万人死于酒精和尼古丁的使用。马赫什·塔卡尔和团队找出了饮酒与吸烟常常相关的原因。他说，这一认识可能帮助人们戒除对酒精和尼古丁的依赖。研究者把结果发表在《神经化学杂志》上。

讲座三（第 23—25 题）

直到不久前，肯尼亚的盲人和视障学生还在用盲文书籍学习。但肯尼亚的盲人学校现在开始采用能以听觉形式提供材料的技术——并在这个过程中拓展了他们的机会。

卢卡斯·蒙齐亚专注地在网上搜索信息。今天的课是生物。蒙齐亚有视觉障碍，过去两年一直在蒂卡盲人学校上电脑课。蒙齐亚读八年级，由于视力问题他很晚才入学。他说，这项技术开辟了过去无法进入的新天地。

「盲文书很贵，买一本要花不少钱，」蒙齐亚解释说，「但现在有了电脑，我们几乎不花钱就能拿到这些书。我们下载各种书来读，读完就关掉程序。」

这所学校六年前引入了辅助技术，使盲人和视障学生能够从电脑和 iPad 上获取信息。学校的一位老师扎卡里·穆伊扎天生失明。他教学生使用这项技术已有约两年。他说，这项技术带来的机会能让他的学生站在同一起跑线上。

「辅助技术让学习者掌握很多技能，真正使他们在生活中独立，」他说，「他们能自己阅读书籍、杂志、报纸这类材料。除此之外，辅助技术还赋予他们可就业的技能。」

一所学校安装这套辅助技术要花 1000 美元，但一家名为「Enable」的非政府组织免费提供给这些学校。Enable 的项目经理彼得·奥奥说，使用这项技术的盲人学生升入高一级学校时仍可能遇到困难。

「学生从小学升到高中、再升到大学时，到了大学就发现没有那套技术。事实是他们在中小学学了那套技术，到了大学却又回到盲文，这对他们来说是又一个挑战。」

到目前为止，肯尼亚 11 所盲人学校中有 4 所采用了这项技术。Enable 表示将为其余学校提供资金加入。

题目

16. 研究人员关于咖啡发现了什么？
17. 关于这项研究我们了解到什么？
18. 关于弗兰克·胡我们了解到什么？
19. 这项研究受到什么批评？
20. 吸烟与饮酒之间是什么关系？
21. 关于尼古丁我们知道什么？
22. 这项新研究的意义何在？
23. 关于蒙齐亚我们了解到什么？
24. 穆伊扎如何评价这项辅助技术？
25. 使用这项技术的人可能面临什么挑战？

title: Test 3 · 讲座或讲话
en:
Lecture One (Questions 16–18)

What is the best way to catch someone who is telling a lie? For a long time, the traditional method of identifying liars was to watch their body language, including facial expressions. What if the person appears to be nervous? Is the person unable to look me in the eye? Is he or she looking around the room? What about other nervous movements? Many people, from parents to police officers and airport security personnel, depend on this method. But does a person's body and face reveal the truth?

Actually, using body language and facial expressions to catch someone in a lie is really hard. And it only works seemingly by chance. According to a new study carried out by researchers in the United Kingdom, talking is the best way to smoke out a liar. The study found that certain conversation-based techniques can help you recognize when a person is lying to you. Like many methods, this conversation method has a name. It is called controlled cognitive engagement, or CCE for short.

The investigation took place at one place where lying can get you into big trouble: an airport. The researchers asked volunteers to pretend they were real passengers and then lie to airport security agents. Some of the agents used spoken, conversation-based methods to question these make-believe passengers. Others depended instead on the person's body language, like lack of eye contact and showing signs of nervousness. The agents talking with the passengers were 20 times more likely to catch the liars.

Here are some tips for catching a liar by using the conversational CCE method.

One, use open-ended questions. These are the opposite of yes-and-no questions. Open-ended questions force the person to stretch the story of their lies until they get caught in their own web of lies.

Two, use the element of surprise. Ask questions they may not think you are going to ask. Ask questions that are surprising or off-topic. This will make it harder for them to keep lying. Or better still, ask them to retell an event backwards in time, going from the most recent event to the earliest. This is hard enough to do with the truth, let alone a story of lies.

Three, watch for changes in confidence and speaking styles. Liars will often change their speaking style when they are questioned. For example, when they feel in control they may be very talkative, but if they feel they are losing control, they may not talk much at all.

Lecture Two (Questions 19–21)

Hello, I'm Steve Ember. Today we tell about a man known as Johnny Appleseed. His real name was John Chapman.

Little is known about John Chapman's childhood. When he was old enough to leave home, he slowly traveled south and west from Massachusetts to the state of Pennsylvania. He is said to have cleared land and planted apple seeds near a waterway. In a short time, the seeds grew to become trees that produced fruit.

Pennsylvania was the first stop in what would become a lifelong effort to plant apple trees. After a few years, Chapman left the hills of western Pennsylvania and traveled west into the Ohio Valley. He planted apple seeds in several areas near a place called Licking Creek.

Chapman planted with thoughts about future markets for his crops. His trees often grew in land near settlements. He often sold his apple seeds to settlers. Sometimes he gave away trees to needy settlers. When low on seeds, he returned east to Pennsylvania to get more. He got the seeds from apple presses — machines used to make apples into a drink called apple cider. Before long, Chapman's trees were growing in fields across Ohio. People began calling him Johnny Appleseed.

Johnny Appleseed was a small man with lots of energy. He had long, dark hair; his eyes were black and bright. He never married. He lived very simply. For years he traveled alone in the wilderness without a gun or knife. He slept in the open air and did not wear shoes on his feet. Some people gave him clothing as payment for his apple trees, but sometimes he wore a large cloth bag or sack as clothing. The sack had holes for his head and arms. On his head he wore a metal container for a hat; he also used this pot for cooking his food.

People said he lived this way because he wanted to. He had enough money for shelter and clothes if he had wanted to buy these things, but he used his money to improve his apple business and help other people. He was famous for his gentleness and bravery. Both settlers and Native Americans liked him. Everywhere he traveled, he was welcomed. Reports from that period suggest that some Native Americans believed he was touched by God.

Lecture Three (Questions 22–25)

Bad news for the delivery guys: you might have to start thinking about finding a new job very soon, because delivery men bringing items to home may become a thing of the past one day. Well, I may have exaggerated the situation a little bit, but what I'm going to tell you next is dead true.

A robot that can drive itself on sidewalks to make door-to-door deliveries is going to be tried out in London and some as-yet-undisclosed US cities in the coming months. Here is a picture of the small black-and-white, slightly rounded machine on six wheels — a brand-new product of the London-based developer Starship Technologies. It can blend in with pedestrian traffic.

Lightweight, it can only carry a small amount in its top compartment: two grocery bags, or small packages up to nine kilograms. The company's chief executive officer, who also co-founded Skype, said the unnamed robot is practical, safe and environmentally friendly.

A user would place an order online as people do right now, but instead of getting the delivery by somebody coming up to and knocking on your door, you would get it by a robot. The electric rover isn't made for long distances. Moving at 6.5 kilometers per hour — that's four miles per hour — it can travel up to five kilometers, and from a local store or retail outlet it can complete deliveries within a half hour.

An advantage for customers is that we can use a smartphone app to decide when we want deliveries to arrive. We call up the delivery using our smartphone, and then the robot gets loaded with our parcel and drives to our doorstep. Once the robot gets moving, using a navigation system that also helps it avoid pedestrians, the customer can use the smartphone app to track it and, upon arrival, unlock the compartment.

You must be thinking about thieves, aren't you? Actually, a lot of thought has been put into protecting the robot from thievery. The robot has nine cameras and GPS. There's an operator who can actually talk to the people around the robot, so there's a loudspeaker in the robot.

I just can't wait to make an order and have it delivered to my doorstep by a robot. I mean, anything would be okay; I just want more contact with the robot than the package itself.

Questions

16. What is the best way to catch a liar, according to the speaker?
17. What do we learn about the investigation mentioned in the lecture?
18. What does the conversational CCE method include, according to the speaker?
19. Where did John Chapman start planting apple trees?
20. What does the speaker say about John Chapman's life?
21. According to the speaker, how did John Chapman spend his money?
22. What does the speaker say about delivery in the future?
23. What do we learn about the robot from the lecture?
24. How far can the robot travel at one time?
25. What has been done to the robot to protect it from thieves?
zh:
讲座一（第 16—18 题）

识破说谎者最好的办法是什么？长期以来，识别说谎者的传统方法是观察他们的肢体语言，包括面部表情。如果这个人看起来很紧张呢？他是不是不敢跟我对视？他是不是在房间里东张西望？还有别的紧张动作吗？从父母到警察、再到机场安检人员，很多人都依赖这种方法。可是，人的身体和脸真能揭示真相吗？

实际上，用肢体语言和面部表情识破谎言非常困难，而且似乎只是碰巧有效。英国研究人员的一项新研究发现，「谈话」才是揪出说谎者的最好办法。研究发现，某些基于对话的技巧能帮你判断一个人是否在对你说谎。和许多方法一样，这种谈话方法也有名字，叫做「受控认知投入」，简称 CCE。

这项调查是在一个说谎会给你带来大麻烦的地方进行的：机场。研究人员请志愿者假扮真实旅客，然后对机场安检人员说谎。一部分安检人员用口头、基于对话的方法询问这些假旅客；另一些人则依赖对方的肢体语言，比如缺乏眼神交流、表现出紧张的迹象。与旅客交谈的那些安检人员抓到说谎者的可能性要高出 20 倍。

以下是运用对话式 CCE 方法识破谎言的一些技巧。

第一，使用开放式问题。这类问题与「是/否」问题相反。开放式问题迫使对方把谎言的故事越编越长，直到被自己编的谎话网住。

第二，运用出其不意。问一些他们没想到你会问的问题，问一些出人意料或离题的问题。这会让他们更难继续说谎。更好的做法是，请他们把一件事倒着时间顺序复述一遍，从最近发生的说到最早的。就算是真事，这样复述也不容易，更不用说编造的谎言了。

第三，留意自信程度和说话风格的变化。说谎者被问到时，往往会改变说话风格。例如，当他们觉得掌控局面时，可能非常健谈；但一旦觉得失去掌控，就可能几乎不说话。

讲座二（第 19—21 题）

大家好，我是史蒂夫·恩伯。今天我们讲一个被称为「苹果佬约翰尼」的人。他的真名叫约翰·查普曼。

关于约翰·查普曼的童年，人们知之甚少。到了可以离家的年纪，他从马萨诸塞州一路缓慢地向南、向西，来到宾夕法尼亚州。据说他在一条水道附近开垦土地、播下苹果种子。不久，种子长成了结出果实的树。

宾夕法尼亚是这项将持续一生的种苹果事业的起点。几年后，查普曼离开宾夕法尼亚西部的丘陵，向西进入俄亥俄河谷。他在一个叫利金溪的地方附近的几片区域播下苹果种子。

查普曼种树时考虑的是将来作物的销路。他的树常常长在定居点附近的土地上。他常把苹果种子卖给定居者，有时也把树送给贫困的定居者。种子不够时，他就东回宾夕法尼亚去取。他从苹果压榨机里获取种子——那种机器把苹果压成一种叫苹果酒的饮料。不久，查普曼的树就长满了俄亥俄各地的田野。人们开始叫他「苹果佬约翰尼」。

苹果佬约翰尼个子不高，精力充沛。他留着深色长发，眼睛又黑又亮。他终身未娶，生活极为简朴。多年来，他不带枪也不带刀，独自在荒野中行走。他露天而睡，脚上不穿鞋。有些人拿衣服抵付苹果树的钱，但有时他就把一个大布袋当衣服穿——袋子上挖了洞，露出头和胳膊。他头上戴一个金属容器当帽子，也用这个罐子做饭。

人们说，他这样生活是因为他自己愿意。如果他愿意买，他其实有足够的钱置办住所和衣服，但他把钱用来发展自己的苹果生意、帮助别人。他以温和与勇敢著称，定居者和印第安人都喜欢他。他走到哪里都受到欢迎。那个时期的报道显示，一些印第安人相信他受到了上帝的感召。

讲座三（第 22—25 题）

对快递员来说是个坏消息：你可能很快就要考虑找一份新工作了，因为把物品送到家门口的快递员，有朝一日可能会成为历史。好吧，我可能稍微夸张了一点，但我接下来要讲的绝对是真的。

一台能在人行道上自行行驶、把包裹送到家门口的机器人，将在未来几个月内在伦敦以及美国几个尚未公布的城市的进行试用。这就是那张照片：一台黑白相间、略显圆润、有六个轮子的小机器——它是伦敦开发商「星船科技」的全新产品，能融入行人车流之中。

它很轻，顶部货舱只能装少量东西：两个购物袋，或者不超过九公斤的小包裹。公司首席执行官（也是 Skype 的联合创始人）说，这台尚未命名的机器人实用、安全、环保。

用户像现在一样在网上下一单，但送来的不是上门敲门的快递员，而是一台机器人。这台电动小车不是为长途设计的。它以每小时 6.5 公里（即每小时 4 英里）的速度行驶，一次最远能走五公里；从本地商店或零售点出发，它能在半小时内完成配送。

对顾客的一个好处是，我们可以用手机应用来决定希望什么时候送到。我们用智能手机叫单，机器人装上我们的包裹，然后开到我们家门口。机器人一启动，就靠导航系统行驶，该系统还能帮它避开行人；顾客可以用手机应用追踪它，等它到达时再解锁货舱。

你一定在想小偷的事，对吧？其实，为了保护机器人不被偷，人们已经考虑了很多。机器人有九个摄像头和 GPS；还有一名操作员，能直接跟机器人周围的人说话——所以机器人身上装了喇叭。

我简直等不及要下一单，让机器人送到我家门口。我是说，送什么都行，我只是想跟机器人多接触一下，而不只是那个包裹。

题目

16. 按讲话者的说法，识破说谎者最好的办法是什么？
17. 关于讲座中提到的调查，我们了解到什么？
18. 按讲话者的说法，对话式 CCE 方法包括哪些内容？
19. 约翰·查普曼最初在哪里种苹果树？
20. 讲话者如何描述约翰·查普曼的生活？

chapter: 第4章 讲座或讲话
title: Test 4 · 讲座或讲话
en:
Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

Welcome to Leadership Insider. It is an online course that invites the most thoughtful and influential people in business to contribute answers to questions about careers and leadership. Let me introduce to you Sanjay Sango, the COO of Delos Capital, who will answer the question: how do you stay humble at work?

In today's business environment, confidence is a key attribute for success. However, there is a difference between confidence and assertiveness, and the best professionals are humble enough to know that.

I first learned this lesson in investment banking. Desperately wanting to be taken seriously, I walked around to deceive my colleagues and offered as many opinions to my bosses as I possibly could. This worked for a while, but then my unwarranted confidence led to setbacks in the form of careless mistakes and lack of attention to details, which was noticed by my superiors as well as clients. While it is tough to realize that I was not the financial genius I imagined myself to be, it also taught me to be humble and recognize that I had a lot more work to do to become proficient in my field. As a result, I focused first on improving my craft and actual skills. My fake confidence became genuine, and that evolution has helped me throughout my career.

These four rules can help you blend humility into your professional skills without compromising your career.

First, think twice before acting. Never make an executive decision that you are not really empowered to make, or that is not backed up with sufficient knowledge, just to impress your boss. If you really want to impress your superiors — or if you are a leader and want to impress your team — do your homework first. A bad decision made in the heat of eagerness will hurt your credibility in the long run.

Second, ask plenty of questions. Obviously, not every question goes to your boss's desk, and sometimes it's better to ask your peers or even your juniors first. While we all want to avoid exposing our weaknesses to our colleagues, the reverse also holds true. Your colleagues will respect you for having the guts to admit your lack of knowledge about something.

Third, admit your mistakes and avoid being defensive. I'm not suggesting that you spend weeks apologizing for every oversight, but making a mistake and refusing to admit it does no good. It exhibits insecurity and a lack of professionalism. "Never complain, never explain" is outdated. That's called being stubborn, not confident.

Fourth, create your own professional goals. Setting expectations for yourself and exceeding them is even more satisfying than surpassing someone else's standards — and, in the eyes of an observant superior, an assuring sign that you deserve career advancement.

Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

Hi, I'm Elizabeth Hoffler, Master of Social Work. I am a social worker, a lobbyist and a special assistant to the executive director at the National Association of Social Workers. Today we're going to be talking about becoming a social worker.

Social work is the helping profession. Its primary mission is to enhance human well-being and help meet the basic needs of all people, with a particular focus on those who are vulnerable, oppressed and living in poverty. We often deal with complex human needs. Social work is different from other professions because we focus on the person and environment. We deal with the external factors that impact a person's situation and outlook, and we create opportunities for assessment and intervention to help clients and communities cope effectively with reality — and change that reality when necessary.

In thousands of ways, social workers help other people. People from every age, every background, across the country — wherever needed, social workers come to help. The most well-known aspect of the profession is that of a social safety net. We help guide people to critical resources and counsel them on life-changing decisions.

There are more than 600,000 professional social workers in the country, and we all either have a bachelor's degree, a master's degree or a PhD in social work. There are more clinically trained social workers than clinically trained psychiatrists, psychologists and psychiatric nurses combined.

Throughout this series you will learn more about the profession, the necessary steps to get a social work degree, the rich history of social work, and the many ways that social workers help others. Later in this series, you'll hear from Stacey Collins and Mel Wilson, fellow social workers at the National Association of Social Workers. Stacey is going to walk you through the step-by-step process of becoming a social worker, and Mel will tell you about the range of options you have once you get your social work degree, as well as the high standards of responsibility the social workers must adhere to.

The National Association of Social Workers represents nearly 145,000 social workers across the country. Our mission is to promote, protect and advance the social work profession. We hope you enjoy this series about how you can make a difference by becoming a social worker. Next we're going to talk about choosing social work.

Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

It's not always easy to tell what's best to do: renting or buying a home. We tend to assume that buying is always better, and the American Dream is at least historically built on that all-important goal of owning your own home. Yet if the housing crash and recession of the last several years have taught us anything, it's that owning a home isn't always all that it's admired to be. And renting can protect you against some of the negative things about the commitment of home ownership.

With all of that in mind, here are some guidelines to consider whether renting or buying is best for you.

Look at the time that you are planning on spending in one place. Most experts advise that if you want to buy, you need to plan to be in the home at least five years, and that time period might be longer depending on market conditions. Think about how committed you are to being in a particular neighborhood, town or state, and use this as your first guide to whether you should buy a home there or not.

Second, buying a home, especially in today's market, can require a significant down payment — often 20% or more of the purchase price. You need to have this amount saved up and be ready to put it down on the house. If you'd rather have the cash on hand for emergencies, college money, vacations or other uses, you might want to think twice about buying a house at this point.

Third, unlike renting, home ownership is an investment. You own the home, and if it goes up in value, your investment grows. Homes don't always appreciate in value, however, and sometimes, as recent years have shown, they can depreciate significantly, leaving homeowners unable to make payments or putting them heavily in debt. When evaluating the investment potential of home ownership, therefore, you must take into account the home you're thinking of buying, the market, and the price you're getting the home for. Consider meeting a financial advisor to go over the figures and determine whether buying a house is a good investment for you or not.

Choosing whether to rent or buy is one of the most important decisions in your life, so make sure to take time and consider all factors before making it.

Questions

16. What do we know about Leadership Insider?
17. What kind of setback did the speaker experience in investment banking?
18. What is the consequence of a bad decision made in the heat of eagerness?
19. What does refusal to admit one's mistake indicate?
20. What do social workers mainly do?
21. What do professional social workers have in common, according to the speaker?
22. What is Mel Wilson going to talk about in the series?
23. What can we learn from the housing crash and recession of the last several years?
24. What is the first guide to decide whether to buy or rent a home?
25. What does the speaker suggest to evaluate the investment potential of home ownership?
zh:
讲座一（第 16—19 题）

欢迎来到《领导力内参》。这是一门在线课程，邀请商界最有思想、最有影响力的人来回答有关职业与领导力的问题。让我介绍桑杰·桑戈，德洛斯资本的首席运营官，他将回答这个问题：在工作中如何保持谦逊？

在当今的商业环境中，自信是成功的关键特质。不过，自信与强势之间是有区别的，最优秀的专业人士谦逊到足以明白这一点。

我最初是在投行学到这一课的。当时我迫切希望被人认真对待，于是四处走动、想让同事对我另眼相看，还尽可能多地向老板提意见。这管用了一阵，但随后我那份没有根据的自信带来了挫折——粗心的错误和对细节的疏忽，被上司和客户都看在了眼里。意识到自己并不是想象中的金融天才虽然难受，但也教会我谦逊，让我认识到要在本领域精通还有大量功课要做。于是我首先专注于打磨手艺和实际技能，虚假的自信变成了真正的自信，这一转变在我的整个职业生涯中都帮到了我。

以下四条规则能帮你在不损害职业发展的前提下，把谦逊融入专业技能。

第一，三思而后行。绝不要为了给老板留下印象，就做出你其实无权做出、或没有足够知识支撑的决策。如果你真想打动上司——或者你是领导者、想打动团队——那就先把功课做足。一时急切之下做出的糟糕决策，长期看会损害你的信誉。

第二，多问问题。显然，不是每个问题都要问到老板桌上，有时先问同辈甚至下属更好。我们都想避免在同事面前暴露弱点，但反过来也同样成立：同事会因为你有勇气承认自己对某件事不了解而尊重你。

第三，承认错误，避免辩解。我不是建议你为每个疏忽道歉好几周，但犯了错却拒不承认毫无好处——那表现出缺乏安全感、缺乏专业精神。「从不抱怨、从不解释」已经过时了，那叫固执，不叫自信。

第四，设定自己的职业目标。为自己设定期望并超越它，比超越别人设定的标准更让人满足——而在善于观察的上司眼里，这也是你值得晋升的可靠迹象。

讲座二（第 20—22 题）

大家好，我是伊丽莎白·霍夫勒，社会工作硕士。我是一名社会工作者、游说者，也是美国社会工作者协会执行主任的特别助理。今天我们要谈的是如何成为一名社会工作者。

社会工作是一个助人的专业。它的首要使命是提升人类福祉，帮助满足所有人的基本需求，尤其关注那些弱势、受压迫和生活在贫困中的人。我们常常要处理复杂的人类需求。社会工作与其他专业不同，因为我们关注「人与环境」。我们处理影响个人处境与心态的外部因素，创造评估和干预的机会，帮助服务对象和社区有效应对现实——并在必要时改变那个现实。

社会工作者以成千上万种方式帮助他人。各种年龄、各种背景的人，遍布全国——哪里需要，社会工作者就到哪里去帮忙。这个专业最广为人知的方面是「社会安全网」：我们帮人找到关键资源，为改变人生的决定提供咨询。

全国有 60 多万名专业社会工作者，我们全都拥有社会工作的学士、硕士或博士学位。受过临床训练的社会工作者，比受过临床训练的精神科医生、心理学家和精神科护士加起来还多。

在这个系列中，你将了解更多关于这个专业的知识、取得社工学位所需的步骤、社会工作丰富的历史，以及社会工作者帮助他人的多种方式。在系列的后半部分，你将听到全国社工协会的同行斯泰西·柯林斯和梅尔·威尔逊的分享。斯泰西会带你一步步走过成为社会工作者的流程，梅尔则会告诉你拿到社工学位后有哪些选择，以及社会工作者必须遵守的高标准责任要求。

美国社会工作者协会代表着全国近 14.5 万名社会工作者。我们的使命是促进、保护并推进社会工作专业。希望你喜欢这个系列，了解如何通过成为社会工作者来带来改变。接下来我们要谈的是「选择社会工作」。

讲座三（第 23—25 题）

要判断租房还是买房更好，并不总是那么容易。我们往往认为买房总是更好，而「美国梦」至少从历史上说就建立在这个至关重要的目标上——拥有自己的房子。然而，如果说过去几年的房市崩盘和经济衰退教会了我们什么，那就是：拥有房产并不总是人们称赞的那样美好。而租房可以让你避开拥有房产这一承诺所带来的一些负面问题。

考虑到这一切，以下是判断租房还是买房更适合你的一些准则。

先看自己计划在同一个地方待多久。多数专家建议，如果想买房，就要计划至少在这套房子里住五年，而且视市场情况，这个期限可能更长。想一想你对某个社区、城镇或州的归属感有多强，并把它作为判断是否该在那里买房的第一条准则。

第二，买房——尤其在当今市场——可能需要一笔数额可观的首付，往往是房价的 20% 甚至更多。你需要攒下这笔钱，并准备好把它投到房子上。如果你更愿意把现金留在手边，用于应急、子女教育、度假或其他用途，那么此刻买房也许要再想想。

第三，与租房不同，拥有房产是一种投资。房子属于你，如果它升值，你的投资就增值。然而，房子并不总是升值；有时正如近几年所示，它们会大幅贬值，让房主无力还贷、或背上沉重债务。因此，在评估拥有房产的投资潜力时，你必须考虑你想买的这套房子、市场行情，以及你买入的价格。可以考虑找一位理财顾问核对数字，判断买房对你是不是一笔好投资。

选择租房还是买房是人生中最重要的决定之一，所以务必花时间、考虑所有因素之后再作决定。

题目

16. 关于《领导力内参》我们了解到什么？
17. 讲话者在投行经历了什么样的挫折？
18. 一时急切之下做出的糟糕决策会有什么后果？
19. 拒不承认错误说明了什么？
20. 社会工作者主要做什么？
21. 按讲话者的说法，专业社会工作者有什么共同点？
22. 梅尔·威尔逊在系列中要讲什么？
23. 从过去几年的房市崩盘和经济衰退中我们能学到什么？
24. 判断买房还是租房的第一条准则是什么？
25. 关于评估拥有房产的投资潜力，讲话者有什么建议？

title: Test 5 · 讲座或讲话
en:
Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

A United Nations agency estimates that 516 million of the world's women cannot read and write. The UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, UNESCO, says programs are needed to help illiterate women learn although they are past school age. Women make up two-thirds of all illiterate adults. The majority of these women live in West Africa.

Many girls in that area never go to school, but in Liberia, a new education program is giving women in their thirties, forties and fifties another chance to learn to read and write.

Pauline Rose heads UNESCO's worldwide monitoring report on Education for All. She says being illiterate causes huge problems in daily life. She notes situations like not being able to read directions on a medicine bottle or the number on a bus. So there are real practical concerns when women are illiterate.

Miss Rose says illiteracy affects not only the women but also their families. Because women are often the main caregivers of children, she says, when women are illiterate, they are less likely to use health services.

Some countries, like Senegal, have improved women's literacy rates through government efforts. They tell more girls in primary school and community programs about the importance of education. But there are still many nations where less than one in four women can read and write. They include Niger, Benin, Mali and Burkina Faso.

Ms. Rose says these countries need literacy programs that target women. She says there is a huge need for illiterate young women and adults to have a second chance to read and write.

Liberia, for example, has launched a "second chance" literacy campaign to teach women. The students never went to school, or they were forced to leave school because of ten years of civil war in the country. Lonnie Smith is 35 years old. She is a student at the adult literacy school at the Firestone Liberia natural rubber company in Margibi County. Her parents did not send her to school, and she could not read or write. Now she is in the first grade and has those skills. She sells her goods at the market and can now count her profit without help. She says having a second chance at education has changed her life: "Today I am a happy woman. I'm very proud."

Liberia's Ministry of Education says 5,000 women currently study in adult literacy programs across the country.

Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

Japan and Germany have the world's oldest populations, but neither country has enough trained health care workers to meet the needs of older adults. So they are turning to Vietnam for help.

This month, 100 young Vietnamese are going to Germany as part of a project to train what are called geriatric nurses — who provide health care services to the elderly — to work in the European country. The trainees recently completed a six-month language and culture class in Hanoi. They will spend the next two years in an occupational training program. If the trainees pass the final exam, they will be able to work in Germany as geriatric nurses for another three years.

Germany is facing a crisis as low birth rates combine with a growing population of citizens who are living longer. About 20% of the population is over the age of 65, and that percentage is expected to continue rising. This is a problem Japan also faces.

Later this year, 150 Vietnamese candidates will go to Japan for two years of training at the country's hospitals. After that, they are expected to take the national nursing exam. Japan already trains nurses from the Philippines and Indonesia, but the health care system has been criticized for being too restrictive. All candidates must take the same exam, but it is very difficult for foreign applicants because few can speak the Japanese language.

Yoko Tsuya is the first secretary at Japan's embassy in Hanoi. She says foreign nationals are given some help to complete the test, like being given more time to answer questions. To improve training, the government plans to combine language classes with real-life experience on the job.

Even with an aging population, many Japanese are opposed to foreigners working in some industries. Critics say foreign labor could lead to higher unemployment, but there is little opposition to foreign nurses.

In Vietnam, the situation is very different. 60% of the population was born after the Vietnam War ended in 1975. There are not yet enough jobs for everyone who wants one. Most children are expected to care for their aging parents when they get old.

Huong Thi Ti, a nurse trainee, thinks that in the future Vietnam will need more hospitals for its elderly. But she adds, learning the skills overseas can help the Vietnamese develop this area for themselves.

Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

The first year of college is usually a time to learn and have fun. Many young people enjoy the freedom of living away from home for the first time. For young women in the United States, however, it is a time when they are at high risk of experiencing a sex crime.

The US Justice Department reports that American women aged 18 to 24 had the highest rate of sexual assault. The study also found that university students were less likely to report such crimes than non-students. Among college women, nine out of 10 knew the person who sexually assaulted them.

In Canada, three universities recently ran a program to train female students to avoid sexual assault while in college. The program was a two-year training course which involved women in their first year of college. The students spent 12 hours learning how to judge risks, deal with emotions and use self-defense. The program taught students to be especially on guard at parties and other high-risk campus social events.

The training taught students to attend such events together. If separated, they should check on each other every now and then. They should also take extra care in their use of alcohol. At least half of the sexual assaults among college women involved drinking.

About 450 students received the training. A group of about the same size received only written information and a brief meeting with the trainers. The group that received the 12 hours of training saw an almost 50% drop in risk of rape.

In the US, Harvard and several other universities have also developed bystander training. This means students offer help if they see someone in danger of being assaulted. The training helps students, both men and women, decide when it is safe to personally intervene and when to call the police.

Last year, the President ordered the establishment of a task force on sexual violence at universities. The investigation report advised universities to take several measures. They include methods for researching the sex-crime climate of the university and improving systems for reporting crimes, as well as prevention programs. The White House task force said one in five women experiences sexual assault in her college years. It has started a website called "Not Alone" to give schools and students information on how to react to and prevent sexual assault.

Questions

16. What do we learn about women and illiteracy from the lecture?
17. What problem might illiterate women encounter?
18. What does Senegal do to improve women's literacy rates?
19. What do we learn about Lonnie Smith?
20. What do we know about the Vietnamese trainees in Germany?
21. What does Japan do to help the foreign trainees?
22. What can we learn about Vietnam from the lecture?
23. What can we learn from the US Justice Department report?
24. What did the Canadian students learn from the program?
25. What did the White House task force do to prevent sexual assaults?

讲座一（第 16—19 题）

联合国一个机构估计，全世界有 5.16 亿女性不会读也不会写。联合国教科文组织（UNESCO）表示，需要开展项目帮助这些已经过了学龄的文盲女性学习。在全世界成年文盲中，女性占三分之二，其中大多数生活在西非。

那一地区的许多女孩从未上过学，但在利比里亚，一项新的教育计划正给三四十岁、五十多岁的女性第二次学会读写的机会。

保琳·罗斯负责教科文组织关于「全民教育」的全球监测报告。她说，不识字会在日常生活中造成巨大问题。她举例说，比如看不懂药瓶上的说明，或看不懂公交车上的编号。所以女性不识字确实存在实际的困难。

罗斯女士说，文盲不仅影响女性本人，也影响她们的家庭。她说，由于女性往往是孩子的主要照顾者，女性不识字时，她们使用医疗服务的可能性就更低。

一些国家如塞内加尔，通过政府努力提高了女性识字率：他们让更多小学女生和社区项目了解教育的重要性。但仍有不少国家只有不到四分之一的女性会读写，包括尼日尔、贝宁、马里和布基纳法索。

罗斯女士说，这些国家需要针对女性的扫盲项目。她说，文盲的年轻女性和成年人极其需要第二次学会读写的机会。

例如，利比里亚发起了一场「第二次机会」扫盲运动来教女性识字。这些学员从未上过学，或因国内十年内战而被迫辍学。朗妮·史密斯 35 岁，是马吉比县凡士通利比里亚天然橡胶公司成人扫盲学校的学生。父母没送她上学，她不识字。现在她读一年级，掌握了读写技能。她在市场上卖货，现在能自己算利润了。她说，第二次受教育的机会改变了她的生活：「今天我很快乐，我非常自豪。」

利比里亚教育部称，目前全国有 5000 名女性在成人扫盲项目中学习。

讲座二（第 20—22 题）

日本和德国拥有世界上老龄化程度最高的人口，但两国都没有足够的受过培训的医护人员来满足老年人的需求。于是它们向越南求助。

本月，100 名越南年轻人前往德国，参加一个培训「老年护理员」（为老年人提供医疗照护服务的人员）的项目，之后在欧洲国家工作。这些学员最近在河内完成了为期六个月的语言与文化课程，接下来将参加为期两年的职业培训项目。如果通过最终考试，他们就能在德国做三年老年护理员。

由于出生率低、寿命长的公民人数不断增加，德国正面临危机。约 20% 的人口超过 65 岁，这一比例预计还会继续上升。日本也面临同样的问题。

今年晚些时候，150 名越南候选人将前往日本，在日本医院接受两年培训，之后参加全国护士资格考试。日本已经在培训来自菲律宾和印度尼西亚的护士，但该国的医疗体系被批评过于排外。所有考生必须参加同一场考试，但对外国考生来说非常困难，因为很少有人会说日语。

津谷洋子是日本驻河内大使馆的一等秘书。她说，外国考生在考试中会得到一些帮助，比如获得更多答题时间。为改进培训，政府计划把语言课程与岗位上的实际经验结合起来。

即便面临人口老龄化，许多日本人仍反对外国人在某些行业工作。批评者说，外国劳动力可能导致失业率上升；不过对外国护士的反对声音不大。

在越南，情况很不一样。60% 的人口是在 1975 年越战结束后出生的。目前还没有足够的工作岗位提供给所有想工作的人。多数子女被期望在父母年老时照顾他们。

护理学员黄氏娣认为，将来越南需要更多面向老年人的医院。但她补充说，在海外学到的技能能帮助越南人自己发展这一领域。

讲座三（第 23—25 题）

大学第一年通常是学习与玩乐的时光。许多年轻人第一次享受离家的自由。然而对美国年轻女性来说，这也是她们遭遇性犯罪风险很高的时期。

美国司法部报告称，18 至 24 岁的美国女性遭遇性侵的比例最高。研究还发现，大学生比非学生更不可能举报这类犯罪。在大学女生中，十个人里有九个认识性侵她们的人。

在加拿大，三所大学最近开展了一个培训女大学生防范性侵的项目。该项目是为期两年的培训课程，参与者是大一女生。学生用 12 小时学习如何判断风险、处理情绪以及使用自卫术。项目教导学生在派对和其他高风险校园社交活动中格外警惕。

培训教导学生参加这类活动时要结伴同行；如果被分开，要时不时互相确认情况。她们还应格外注意饮酒——大学女生遭遇的性侵中至少一半与饮酒有关。

约 450 名学生接受了培训；人数大致相当的另一组只收到书面材料，并与培训者短会一次。接受 12 小时培训的那组，遭强奸的风险下降了近 50%。

在美国，哈佛等几所大学还开展了「旁观者培训」。这意味着学生如果看到有人面临被侵犯的危险，就要提供帮助。培训帮助男女学生判断何时可以安全地亲自介入、何时应当报警。

去年，总统下令成立大学性暴力问题特别工作组。调查报告建议大学采取若干措施，包括研究校园性犯罪氛围的方法、改进犯罪举报系统，以及预防项目。白宫特别工作组称，五分之一的女性在大学期间遭遇过性侵。它开设了一个名为「你并不孤单」的网站，向学校和学生们提供如何应对和预防性侵的信息。

题目

16. 从讲座中我们了解到女性和文盲的什么情况？
17. 文盲女性可能遇到什么问题？
18. 塞内加尔如何提高女性识字率？
19. 关于朗妮·史密斯我们了解到什么？
20. 关于在德国的越南学员我们了解到什么？
21. 日本如何帮助外国学员？
22. 从讲座中我们了解到越南的什么情况？
23. 从美国司法部的报告我们能了解到什么？
24. 加拿大学生在项目中学到了什么？
25. 白宫特别工作组为预防性侵做了什么？

chapter: 第5章 综合训练
title: Model Test 1 · 综合训练
en:
Section A — Conversation One (Questions 1–4)

— Do you think you can give an exact definition of management, Mr. Rogers?
— Management is the process of achieving results through other people.
— What are the functions of management?
— There are mainly four. The first is planning. Managers define goals, establish strategy and develop plans to coordinate activities.
— That's not easy, I think.
— No. And the second is organizing, which means managers will determine what tasks are to be done, who is to do them, how the tasks are to be grouped, who reports to whom, etc.
— That's complicated.
— And the third is leading. It includes motivating subordinates, directing others, selecting the most effective communication channels, and resolving conflicts.
— Do you think the goal of good management is to get rid of conflicts?
— Actually, we've made considerable progress towards overcoming the view that conflict is bad.
— So you mean conflicts can be good for an organization?
— Yes. Conflicts can be used to bring about substantial changes to the existing power structure, current patterns of interaction between people at work, and attitudes.
— That surprises me.
— The last function, controlling, means to monitor activities to ensure they are being accomplished as planned and to correct significant deviations.
— It is said that all managers need to realize that the more they delegate now, the less time it will take to accomplish tasks later. Is that true?
— Right. Without delegation, managers run the risk of being a doer rather than a manager.
— Can I understand this as delegation is a ticket to ride free and have others do your work?
— Not exactly. It is rather a means for managers to focus on their true functions.

Section A — Conversation Two (Questions 5–8)

— Interested in this book? This is our bestseller this week.
— Bestseller. I'm considering what new ideas it gives about how to deal with aggravating people.
— It asks people to quit complaining and do something. What surprises many people about this book is it suggests that the best thing to do is to change yourself, because you are not going to change the other person.
— Really? It's me that has to change, as opposed to the other person?
— Well, have you ever changed anybody?
— I've tried many times. It's not really possible, though.
— That's right.
— But how can I do that?
— The book is here. Bring it back home and read it, and you can find the answer.
— Before I pay my money, I should be clear that this book is useful for me. I don't want to pay for it and then find I have paid for nothing.
— This book is definitely worth the money. The book even tells you how to deal with different types of workers, coworkers and bosses — from the most common annoying type to the worst kind.
— Give me the most common annoying type of coworker.
— The most common annoying type of coworker is called a "boundary buster." It's someone who invades your space, makes too much noise, eats up your time, or chews your ear off. They are boundary busters.
— And how do I deal with them?
— Again, sir, the book is here. Bring it back and read for the answer.
— It seems you know a lot about this book. Can I draw the conclusion that you fancy it?
— Well, frankly, I am the author.

Section B — Passage One (Questions 9–11)

Last summer I went through a training program and became a literacy volunteer. The training I received, though excellent, did not tell me how it was to work with a real student. When I began to discover what other people's lives were like because they could not read, I realized the true importance of reading.

My first student, Marie, was a 44-year-old single mother of three. In the first lesson, I found out that she walked two miles to the nearest supermarket twice a week because she didn't know which bus to take. When I told her I would get her a bus schedule, she told me it would not help because she could not read it. She said she also had difficulty once she got to the supermarket because she couldn't always remember what she needed. Since she did not know words, she could not write out a shopping list. Also, she could only recognize items by sight, so if the product had a different label, she would not recognize it as the product she wanted.

As we worked together, learning how to read built Marie's self-confidence, which encouraged her to continue in her studies. She began to make rapid progress and was even able to take the bus to the supermarket. At the end of the program, she began helping her youngest son, Tony, a shy first grader, with his reading.

As a literacy volunteer, I learned a great deal about teaching and helping others. In fact, I may have learned more from the experience than Marie did.

Section B — Passage Two (Questions 12–15)

In the past, industries had more freedom than they have now, and they did not need to be as careful as they must today. They did not need to worry a lot about the safety of the new products that they developed. They did not have to pay much attention to the health and safety of the people who worked for them. Often new products were dangerous for the people who used them. Often conditions in the workplace had very bad effects on the health of the workers.

Of course, sometimes there were real disasters which attracted the attention of government and which showed the need for changes. Also, scientists who were doing research into the health of the workers sometimes produced information which governments could not ignore. At such times there were inquiries into the causes of the disaster or the problems. New safety rules were often introduced as a result of these inquiries. However, the new rules came too late to protect the people who had died or become seriously ill.

Today, many governments have special departments which protect customers and workers. In the US, for example, there is a department which tests new airplanes and gives warnings about possible problems. It also makes the rules that aircraft producers must follow. Another department controls the food and drugs that companies sell. A third department looks at the places where people work and then reports any companies that are breaking laws which protect the health and safety of workers.

Section C — Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

You are invited to a large party. Loud music is playing and lots of people are dancing. Groups of people are mingling with each other, making small talk about many different topics. Which of these people sound most like you? Person A, who tries to talk to everyone and stays late? Or person B, who prefers to talk to only a few people and leaves early?

If you said person A, you are probably more extroverted. If you said person B, you are probably more introverted. Or perhaps you are person C and fall somewhere in the middle.

Introvert and extrovert are two commonly used words to describe a person's personality. And they are also commonly misused and misunderstood.

Introverts may be viewed as quiet, shy and timid. They may be called wallflowers, meaning they are so quiet they blend in with flowers on the wallpaper. Extroverts may be viewed as bold, confident, loud and full of energy. They are often called "alpha," meaning a leader of the group.

Introverted and extroverted people may fit those descriptions. But these same descriptions do not define introversion and extraversion properly.

Introverts and extroverts use their brains differently, and they get their energy differently. Introversion is the state of being mostly concerned with one's own mental life. Extraversion is the opposite: extraversion is the state of being mostly concerned with what is outside oneself.

People who consider themselves introverts may say they need to be alone to charge their batteries, or that being in large crowds makes them tired. However, introverts may still love being social and going to parties. But such activities require time to prepare and time to repair. Extroverts may say, "I don't need alone time; I feel more relaxed being around other people." Even so, extroverts can still feel unsure or not confident among other people.

Susan Cain is the author of "Quiet: The Power of Introverts." In an article published in Psychology Today, she explains that shyness is often considered a synonym of introversion. It is not. Shyness is having a fear of being judged poorly by others. Introverts just prefer being in quiet environments.

For example, Bill Gates, the inventor of Microsoft, is quiet and bookish, she writes. But Gates does not care about the opinions other people may have of him. "He is an introvert," writes Cain, "but he is not shy."

The famous singer and actor Barbra Streisand has an outgoing, larger-than-life personality. But Barbra Streisand, Cain writes, also has a paralyzing case of stage fright. Performers who suffer from stage fright can quite literally be frozen or paralyzed on stage. Cain considers Barbra Streisand a shy extrovert.

Section C — Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

Many people all over the world enjoy an alcoholic drink during dinner. Many people raise a glass of alcohol to celebrate a wedding or a birthday. And having drinks after work with friends and coworkers is called happy hour. All these situations are considered social drinking, because they happen at social events. But when does social drinking become problem drinking?

According to the World Health Organization, alcohol abuse kills 3.3 million people each year. That is six percent of all deaths around the world. And in a new report on alcohol use around the world, the WHO says alcohol can create dependency or addiction in some people. The report also warns that alcohol use can increase the risk of developing more than 200 diseases, including some kinds of cancers. And the WHO says alcohol abuse can put people at greater risk of infectious diseases.

WHO mental health and substance abuse director Shekhar Saxena says the organization is concerned about drinking among young people between the ages of 15 and 19. And it is most concerned about binge drinking, or an extended period of heavy drinking.

The report concludes that worldwide, 16% of drinkers over the age of 15 engage in binge drinking, which is much more harmful than other kinds of drinking. The report warns that more women are drinking alcohol, and the report says women are at greater risk than men for some alcohol-related health conditions.

The report also finds Europe is the area with the highest alcohol use. Central and Eastern Europe are especially high. The WHO says people in Russia, Ukraine and some neighboring countries drink a lot of alcohol and binge drink.

Vladimir Poznyak is the WHO management of substance abuse coordinator. He says less alcohol is used in Africa than in Europe. But he adds the health effects are worse in Africa because of a lack of social support systems such as access to healthcare.

The World Health Organization suggests ways countries can protect people from alcohol abuse. These include increasing taxes on alcohol sales, raising the drinking age limit and controlling the marketing of alcoholic beverages.

Section C — Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

South Africa is the richest country in Africa. It is also one of the most modern and technologically advanced. It has some of the best rail, road and communication systems in Africa. Yet more than two-thirds of South African adults have never used the internet.

The South African Network Society recently reported that only 34% of South African adults use the internet. That is about 12 million people. Three-quarters of the country's internet users live in cities. Most of them use cell phones to get on the internet. The rest go to internet cafes or use the internet at school or work.

Indra de Lanerolle is with the South African Network Society. He says there are many reasons why so few South Africans use the internet. Cost is one of them. "We do have expensive costs, and cost is a big limitation to internet use. It stops some people from using the internet at all, and the other thing is it stops people from using it very much. So unless we can do much better than one in three connected, increasingly that's going to be a real disadvantage for the country."

Poor internet connectivity in rural South Africa and the high prices of internet-ready mobile phones have also kept the poor disconnected. Most schools and workplaces in rural South Africa, where the majority of the country's people live, have no internet connection. And many areas of the country do not have internet cafes.

Sam Gina lives in Johannesburg. He has never been on the internet. "At home I don't have it. A laptop is too expensive for me. Now I am using a phone that doesn't have internet."

Wilson Ayong is a Cameroonian citizen who operates an internet cafe in Johannesburg. He says the prices at internet cafes are too high for many South Africans.

The South African Network Society's Mr. de Lanerolle says internet access in the country is improving. He says a new generation of internet users from the country's middle class is quickly entering an era once reserved for the rich. His belief is supported by reports that show internet usage and access in South Africa has increased by more than 100% in the last five years.

Questions

1. What is management, according to the man?
2. What does the function of organizing include, according to the man?
3. What does the man think of conflicts?
4. Which statement does the man support?
5. What do we learn about the woman?
6. What is surprising about the book the woman recommends?
7. What kind of person is the man?
8. What is a boundary buster?
9. What did the speaker do last summer?
10. How did Marie used to find the goods she wanted in the supermarket?
11. How was Marie's study during the summer?
12. Compared with today's industries, what were the industries in the past like?
13. What did the government do years ago?
14. What does the passage say about industries in the US today?
15. What is the speaker mainly talking about?
16. What kind of behavior is considered more introverted?
17. What is our impression of extroverted people?
18. What do we learn about people who consider themselves introverts?
19. What kind of behavior can be considered shy?
20. What is happy hour?
21. What do we learn about alcohol use from the talk?
22. What does WHO suggest on controlling alcohol use?
23. What do we know about South Africa?
24. What keeps the poor people in South Africa from using the internet?
25. What will be the future development of internet use in South Africa?
zh:
A 节 · 对话一（第 1—4 题）

—— 罗杰斯先生，你认为你能给「管理」下一个确切的定义吗？
—— 管理是通过他人取得成果的过程。
—— 管理有哪些职能？
—— 主要有四项。第一项是计划。管理者要确定目标、制定战略、编制计划来协调活动。
—— 我觉得这不容易。
—— 是不容易。第二项是组织，也就是说，管理者要决定做哪些任务、由谁来做、任务如何分组、谁向谁汇报等等。
—— 这很复杂。
—— 第三项是领导。它包括激励下属、指导他人、选择最有效的沟通渠道、解决冲突。
—— 你认为良好管理的目标是消除冲突吗？
—— 其实，我们在克服「冲突是坏事」这一看法上已经取得了相当大的进展。
—— 所以你的意思是，冲突对一个组织来说可能是好事？
—— 对。冲突可以被用来促成对现有权力结构、人们工作中当前的互动模式以及态度的实质性改变。
—— 这让我很意外。
—— 最后一项职能是控制，就是监控活动，确保按计划完成，并纠正重大偏差。
—— 据说所有管理者都要认识到：现在授权越多，以后完成任务花的时间就越少。这是真的吗？
—— 对。没有授权，管理者就有沦为「办事员」而不是管理者的风险。
—— 我能不能这样理解：授权就是一张可以白拿、让别人替你干活的通行证？
—— 不完全是。它更像是让管理者专注于自己真正职能的一种手段。

A 节 · 对话二（第 5—8 题）

—— 对这本书感兴趣？这是我们本周的畅销书。
—— 畅销书。我正在琢磨它能给出什么新想法，来对付那些让人恼火的人。
—— 它让人别再抱怨，去做点什么。这本书让很多人意外的是，它建议最好的办法是改变你自己，因为你改变不了别人。
—— 真的吗？要改变的是我，而不是对方？
—— 那你改变过谁吗？
—— 我试过很多次，可其实做不到。
—— 没错。
—— 那我该怎么做？
—— 书在这儿，买回去读，你就能找到答案。
—— 在我掏钱之前，我得先弄清楚这书对我有用。我可不想付了钱，最后发现白花了。
—— 这本书绝对值这个钱。书上甚至告诉你如何应付不同类型的员工、同事和老板——从最常见的烦人型到最恶劣的那种。
—— 那就说说最常见的烦人型同事。
—— 最常见的烦人型同事叫「越界者」。就是那种侵占你的空间、弄出太多噪音、占用你的时间、或者拉着你喋喋不休的人。他们就是越界者。
—— 那我怎么应付他们？
—— 还是那句话，先生，书在这儿。买回去读答案。
—— 看来你对这本书很了解。我能不能得出结论：你很喜欢它？
—— 说实话，我就是作者。

B 节 · 篇章一（第 9—11 题）

去年夏天我参加了一个培训项目，成了一名扫盲志愿者。我接受的培训虽然很好，却没有告诉我跟真正的学生一起学习是什么样子。当我开始了解那些不识字的人的生活是什么样时，我才意识到阅读的真正重要性。

我的第一个学生玛丽 44 岁，是三个孩子的单亲母亲。第一堂课上我发现，她每周两次步行两英里到最近的超市，因为她不知道该坐哪路公交车。我告诉她我可以给她一份公交时刻表，她说那没用，因为她看不懂。她说，到了超市也有困难，因为她总是记不住自己要买什么。由于不认字，她没法列购物清单。而且她只能靠样子认商品，所以如果产品换了标签，她就认不出那是她想买的东西。

我们一起学习的过程中，识字建立起了玛丽的自信，这又鼓励她继续学下去。她开始进步很快，甚至能坐公交车去超市了。项目结束时，她开始帮最小的儿子托尼——一个害羞的一年级学生——练阅读。

作为一名扫盲志愿者，我在教学和帮助他人方面学到了很多。事实上，我从这段经历中学到的可能比玛丽还多。

B 节 · 篇章二（第 12—15 题）

过去，工业企业比现在有更多自由，也不必像今天这样小心。它们不需要太担心自己所开发新产品的安全性，不必太在意为其工作的人的健康与安全。新产品常常对使用者有危险，工作场所的条件常常对工人的健康有很坏的影响。

当然，有时会发生真正的灾难，引起政府的注意，表明必须做出改变。此外，研究工人健康的科学家有时也会得出政府无法忽视的信息。这种时候，就会对灾难或问题的原因展开调查。这些调查往往促成了新的安全规定。然而，新规定来得太晚，保护不了那些已经死亡或患上重病的人。

今天，许多国家都有保护消费者和工人的专门部门。例如在美国，有一个部门负责测试新飞机，并就可能出现的问题发出警告，它还制定飞机制造商必须遵守的规则。另一个部门管控公司销售的食品和药品。第三个部门检查人们工作的场所，并举报任何违反保护工人健康与安全法律的公司。

C 节 · 讲座一（第 16—19 题）

你被邀请参加一个大型派对。音乐很响，很多人在跳舞。一群人互相交往，就许多不同话题闲聊。下面这些人里，谁最像你？A：努力跟每个人都聊、而且待到很晚的人？B：只愿意跟少数几个人说话、早早就走的人？

如果你说 A，你可能更外向。如果你说 B，你可能更内向。又或者你是 C，落在中间某处。

「内向」和「外向」是两个常用来描述性格的词，也常被误用和误解。

内向的人可能被认为是安静、害羞、胆怯的，可能被称为「壁花」——意思是他们太安静，跟壁纸上的花融为一体。外向的人可能被认为是胆大、自信、嗓门大、精力充沛的，常被称为「alpha」，意思是群体中的领袖。

内向和外向的人或许符合这些描述，但这些描述并不能恰当定义内向与外向。

内向者和外向者用脑方式不同，获取能量的方式也不同。内向是指主要关注自己内心世界的状态；外向则相反，是主要关注自身之外事物的状态。

自认为内向的人可能会说，他们需要独处来「充电」，或者待在人群里会让他们疲惫。不过，内向的人也可能仍然喜欢社交、喜欢参加派对——只是这类活动需要时间来准备、也需要时间来恢复。外向的人可能会说：「我不需要独处时间，跟别人在一起我更放松。」即便如此，外向的人在人群中也仍可能感到不自信、没把握。

苏珊·凯恩是《安静：内向性格的竞争力》的作者。她在《今日心理学》上发表的一篇文章中解释说，害羞常被视为内向的同义词，其实不是。害羞是害怕被别人负面评价；内向的人只是更喜欢安静的环境。

例如，微软的创始人比尔·盖茨安静、爱读书，她写道。但盖茨并不在乎别人可能怎么看他。「他是个内向的人，」凯恩写道，「但他并不害羞。」

著名歌手兼演员芭芭拉·史翠珊有着外向、气场强大的性格。但凯恩写道，芭芭拉·史翠珊也有严重的、让她动弹不得的怯场。饱受怯场之苦的表演者，真的可能在台上僵住、动弹不得。凯恩把芭芭拉·史翠珊看作「害羞的外向者」。

C 节 · 讲座二（第 20—22 题）

全世界有很多人喜欢在晚餐时喝点酒。很多人举杯庆祝婚礼或生日。下班后跟朋友、同事喝一杯，叫做「欢乐时光」。这些情况都被视为社交饮酒，因为它们发生在社交场合。但社交饮酒什么时候会变成问题饮酒？

据世界卫生组织统计，酗酒每年导致 330 万人死亡，占全世界所有死亡人数的 6%。在一份关于全球饮酒情况的新报告中，世卫组织说，酒精会让一些人产生依赖或成瘾。报告还警告，饮酒会增加罹患 200 多种疾病的风险，包括某些癌症。世卫组织还说，酗酒会让人更容易患上传染病。

世卫组织心理健康与物质滥用司司长谢哈爾·萨克塞纳说，该组织担心 15 至 19 岁年轻人的饮酒问题，最担心的是「狂饮」，即长时间大量饮酒。

报告得出结论：全世界 15 岁以上的饮酒者中有 16% 会狂饮，而狂饮比其他饮酒方式危害大得多。报告警告说，越来越多的女性在饮酒，而且报告称，在某些与酒精相关的健康问题上，女性风险高于男性。

报告还发现，欧洲是酒精使用量最高的地区，中欧和东欧尤其高。世卫组织说，俄罗斯、乌克兰及一些邻国的人饮酒量大，且常狂饮。

弗拉基米尔·波兹尼亚克是世卫组织物质滥用管理协调员。他说，非洲的酒精使用量比欧洲少，但他补充说，由于缺乏社会支持体系（比如获得医疗服务的机会），非洲的健康后果更严重。

世界卫生组织建议各国采取措施保护人们免遭酒精滥用之害，包括提高酒类销售税、提高法定饮酒年龄，以及管控酒精饮料的营销。

C 节 · 讲座三（第 23—25 题）

南非是非洲最富有的国家，也是最现代化、技术最先进的国家之一，拥有非洲最好的铁路、公路和通信系统之一。然而，超过三分之二的南非成年人从未使用过互联网。

南非网络协会最近报告称，只有 34% 的南非成年人使用互联网，约 1200 万人。全国网民中有四分之三住在城市，大多数人用手机上网，其余的人去网吧、或在学校和单位上网。

英德拉·德·拉内罗尔就职于南非网络协会。他说，南非上网的人这么少，原因很多，成本是其中之一。「我们的费用确实很高，成本是上网的一大限制。它让一些人完全没法上网，另一方面，它也让人没法多上网。所以除非我们能把三分之一的上网率大幅提高，否则这越来越会成为这个国家真正的劣势。」

南非农村互联网连接差、可上网手机价格高，也让穷人继续与网络隔绝。南非大多数人居住在农村，而农村的大多数学校和工作场所没有网络连接，全国许多地区也没有网吧。

萨姆·吉纳住在约翰内斯堡，他从未上过网。「家里没有网。笔记本电脑对我来说太贵了。我现在用的手机不能上网。」

威尔逊·阿永是喀麦隆公民，在约翰内斯堡经营一家网吧。他说，网吧的价格对许多南非人来说太高了。

南非网络协会的德·拉内罗尔先生说，南非的互联网接入正在改善。他说，来自中产阶级的新一代网民，正迅速进入一个曾经只属于富人的时代。他的看法得到了报告的印证：报告显示，过去五年南非的互联网使用与接入增长了 100% 以上。

题目

2. 按这位男士的说法，组织职能包括什么？

title: Model Test 2 · 综合训练
